title: Memory, the Self-justifying Historian
coreMove: Before trusting a vivid memory, ask what present innocence the memory is helping protect.
sourcePressure: The chapter treats memory as reconstruction rather than neutral recording; the source supports conflicting recollections, confidence without accuracy, and Anthony Greenwald's "totalitarian ego" metaphor.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Making the chapter a generic warning that memory is fallible, rather than showing memory as an identity-protecting reconstruction.

sourceAnchors.name: Anthony Greenwald
sourceAnchors.detail: the source names Greenwald's "totalitarian ego" as a metaphor for a censoring self-system that favors flattering evidence
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Greenwald's totalitarian ego is not a monster in the basement; it is the quiet editor deciding which parts of the past get to stay bright.

sourceAnchors.name: the self-justifying historian
sourceAnchors.detail: the source names memory as a self-justifying historian that arranges the past into a livable story
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Memory can act less like a camera and more like a house historian paid to keep the family crest clean.

hook: Do not open with childhood nostalgia.
Avoid a generic lost-keys memory trick.
counterintuition: Do not say vivid memories are always false.
Avoid reducing memory to brain storage.
tryThisNow: No "ask someone what they remember" without a specific disputed action.
examples: No courtroom eyewitness scene; save legal pressure for the law chapter.
No repeated couple argument scene; save marriage pressure for ch7.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person direct address, retrospective realization, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

exampleSpecs.domain: siblings reconstructing a hospital visit before dividing care duties for their mother
exampleSpecs.audience: adult siblings whose memories protect different versions of loyalty
exampleSpecs.stakes: one sibling may be cast as selfish because each remembers the visit around their own sacrifice
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Hannah puts the parking receipt, nurse call log, and text thread on the table before deciding whose memory gets to carry blame
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a hospital parking receipt flattened under a water glass

exampleSpecs.domain: a software outage timeline where the product lead remembers warning engineering earlier than the messages show
exampleSpecs.audience: teams rebuilding events after a public incident
exampleSpecs.stakes: the postmortem either learns from timestamps or preserves each role's innocence
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Nicolas drags the chat export beside the outage timeline and marks where his remembered warning appears two hours later than he thought
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a server-status timeline printed with three red outage blocks

exampleSpecs.domain: a co-parenting exchange after a missed school pickup
exampleSpecs.audience: separated parents trying to separate memory from prosecution
exampleSpecs.stakes: the child's schedule becomes another exhibit in a moral case
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Astrid hears herself say "you always do this," then opens the shared calendar and corrects the memory before sending the message
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a child's raincoat dripping onto the hallway mat

exampleSpecs.domain: a landlord deposit dispute over a scratched oak floor
exampleSpecs.audience: people tempted to remember property damage around their preferred innocence
exampleSpecs.stakes: a small dispute hardens into accusations because each side remembers the move-out walk-through differently
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Michael predicts the move-out photos will prove his account, then compares the photo metadata to the inspection sheet before claiming certainty
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a silver key ring beside a scratched strip of oak flooring

exampleSpecs.domain: a surgical handoff review after a missing allergy bracelet
exampleSpecs.audience: clinical teams whose confidence can outrun recorded sequence
exampleSpecs.stakes: a safety fix depends on knowing whether the bracelet was absent, removed, or never checked
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: It takes Paula watching the doorway camera log to separate what she usually does from what she actually did that morning
exampleSpecs.firstImage: an empty plastic bracelet clasp in a specimen tray

exampleSpecs.domain: an amateur choir committee revisiting why a long-time accompanist quit
exampleSpecs.audience: small-group leaders whose recollections protect their own kindness
exampleSpecs.stakes: the committee will repeat the insult if the past stays polished
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: You watch Akira read the resignation email slowly and underline the sentence everyone had remembered as gratitude but that was actually a warning
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a torn concert program tucked inside a piano bench

skillTargets: test vivid memory against external sequence
identify identity protection inside conflicting recollections
evaluate when confidence is evidence versus successful reconstruction

tryThisNowSpec: Pick one conflict memory you tell often; write the one detail that would make you look worse and check whether it is absent, minimized, or disputed.
